## Containment engine versions (cascadeshield runs, same scenario)

Each recovery rule was added because the previous version failed in a measurable way. The `none` and `reactive` runs are shared.

| Version | Session failure | SLO violation (s) | Tutor p95 (s) | Answers from the LLM | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v1 · no recovery probe | 0.8 % | 1 | 0.02 | 2 % | Breaker opened, then the LLM's risk froze just under the threshold with no traffic: the LLM stayed off for the whole exam. |
| v2 · timed probe | 61.1 % | 68 | 16.02 | 12 % | Half-open probes at 10 % of traffic looked calm, the breaker closed, and full traffic re-broke the LLM every ~2 min. |
| v3 · probe + demand gate | 2.4 % | 3 | 3.46 | 11 % | Stays half-open until demand falls below 80 % of the load that broke it; failed recoveries double the wait. |
<!-- fedora:engine-versions end -->

## Dataset and predictor (2026-10-22)

**Dataset:** 60 valid episodes (0 invalid), recorded on Fedora against the platform with the mock LLM
calibrated to the Mac (41 tok/s), `PROTECTION_MODE=none`. 29 360 labelled rows (one per 2 s per service),
25.1 % positive. 35 of 36 "fail" episodes reached a failure onset and 0 of 15 "safe" episodes did.

**Predictor:** Episodes: 60 (48 train / 12 held out). Metrics on `llm_inference` rows of the held-out episodes. Threshold chosen on out-of-fold training scores (≤ 1 false alarm per hour).

| Model | Threshold | PR-AUC | Recall | False alarms / h | Lead median (s) | Lead p10 (s) | Onsets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| lr_v1 | 0.85 | 0.66 | 0.79 | 0.00 | 18 | 14 | 14 |
| rf_v1 | 0.89 | 0.69 | 0.79 | 2.15 | 20 | 14 | 14 |
| xgb_v1 | 0.90 | 0.70 | 0.86 | 1.08 | 19 | 12 | 14 |
| threshold rule (Phase 1) | 0.80 | 0.45 | 0.79 | 3.23 | 24 | 8 | 14 |

## Unseen-fault test (trained without `leak`, tested on `leak` episodes)

Episodes: 54 train / 6 leak. Recall 1.00 over 8 onsets, 0.00 false alarms per hour, PR-AUC 0.61.

Time-to-failure regressor (estimate): MAE 13 s on held-out rows with y = 1.

Reading the table honestly: the ML models beat the Phase 1 threshold rule on PR-AUC (0.66-0.70 vs 0.45) and on
false alarms (0-2.2 vs 3.2 per hour) at the same recall (0.79), but not on median lead time (18-20 s vs 24 s);
their 10th-percentile lead time is better (12-14 s vs 8 s). `rf_v1` is the deployed model (SHAP explanations
need a tree model); its held-out false-alarm rate (2.15/h) is above the 1/h target its threshold was chosen
for on training folds. The deployed `rf_v1` is refitted on all 60 episodes; the same rule then picks a
threshold of 0.95 (0.89 in the held-out table above), and every live run and comparison used 0.95. Unseen-fault caveat: the `leak` fault only holds memory and does not slow the platform,
so the onsets in leak episodes come from overload, not from the leak itself.

<!-- fedora:ablation start (interpretation of the comparison block above; 2 runs per ablation) -->
## Ablation: which part matters (mock LLM, 2 runs each)

- **The degradation ladder matters most.** Limited to L0/L3 (no lean or cache steps), session failure rose
  from 0 % to 37 %, SLO violation from 0 s to 51 s, and all 3 services failed in both runs. The cache + RAG
  step (L2) is what lets students keep getting fast, useful answers while the LLM is protected.
- **The ML predictor adds little over the threshold rule *in this scenario*.** With the same containment
  engine, the Phase 1 threshold risk did almost as well (1.2 % vs 0 % session failure). The offline table
  above shows where ML helps: fewer false alarms at the same recall.
- **The dependency graph cannot show an effect in this ablation, by construction.** The engine acts on the
  LLM's cascade risk, and the LLM has no downstream dependencies, so its cascade risk equals its own risk with
  or without the graph. The graph drives the dashboard's blast radius and the orchestrator/gateway risks, not
  the containment decision; an ablation that matters would need containment acting on gateway risk.
- Two runs per ablation: treat these as directional. The dots in figure 5b show each run.
<!-- fedora:ablation end -->

<!-- fedora:limits start -->
## Known limitations found during evaluation

- **Stale session count (platform, gateway).** `cs_sessions_active` is only recomputed when a request
  arrives, so after load stops it keeps its last value instead of falling to 0 within 60 s as
  `contracts/metrics.md` defines. Effect: after a rush the control room still sees "students online",
  idle risk stays elevated and the half-open demand gate waits longer than needed. Training episodes and
  comparison runs are barely affected (their exports end when the load ends). Fix: prune and set the
  gauge from a periodic task in the gateway, not only in `touch_session`.
- **Cascade risk compounds calibrated floors.** A calibrated model never predicts exactly 0, and
  `R(v) = 1 - (1 - p_v) * prod(1 - w * R(u))` adds those small floors along the chain: at idle, own risks
  of 0.06-0.34 give the gateway a cascade risk of about 0.3-0.5. Containment acts only on the LLM's cascade
  risk (= its own risk), so decisions are unaffected; only the dashboard colours of upstream services are.
<!-- fedora:limits end -->
